title: Nayack (Fort Hamilton)
summary: Nayack is connected with the New Utrecht point of land at present-day Fort Hamilton, directly opposite Staten Island. The history preserves a western Long Island shore name tied to the Narrows and the New Netherland period.
map_geometry_source: approximate modern Fort Hamilton marker for Nayack point; not exact historical boundary
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Identified in 1652 Dutch colonial records as a specific point of land where Manhattan Indians lived, Nayack directly faced Staten Island across the Narrows. Acknowledging these early Indigenous coastal hubs challenges the modern erasure of Native history beneath heavy urban development, reminding us that places like present-day Fort Hamilton were once thriving, strategically important Native American homelands.
history_content: Nayack belongs to the western Long Island shoreline at New Utrecht and Fort Hamilton. Dated New Netherland context appear in the Historic Timeline.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Nayack, Naieck, Najeck, Najack, and Nayack-Point. The name is interpreted as a point or corner of land, a meaning also connected with related names such as Noyack.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place-names are also a key part of the shared language through which we come to understand and navigate the world.”

— Words Are Monuments, What's in a Name? (2024), opening discussion
whereintheworld_content: The map placement is an approximate general point for Fort Hamilton at the southwest corner of Brooklyn, not an exact boundary for the older Nayack land or settlement.
